title: Rehearsals and the sound of Ellington's records
summary: Duke rehearsed before sessions; recordings were exacting.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: So how were the rehearsals in the band? Did you all rehearse a lot?

Oh, yeah. Duke was very exact. He was exact. He would write his dreams. I always called them his dreams, you know. Like numbers he would write, he would write them down, rehearse a couple hours, three hours, a recording session we rehearsed a day, four or five hours and then record. So when we got in the studio, time was valuable. We didn't do a lot of stumbling. We rehearsed a lot. Like we had something important, like to play a concert or play a recording, he would have everything written out. We rehearsed it two or three times so when we first got to the studio, we'd bat it down once for balance and tape it. That's right.
Do you think that he -- I noticed that in listening to the recordings of Ellington's band, you all got a much better recording sound than a lot of other bands.

Yeah, we had a special guy, Bob, I don't know his last name. It wasn't like recording now. It had two notes, there wasn't no one guy off key. This guy -- Duke would stand off, when a guy over there was a little off, he would stop it and correct it. Not like now, all these bums that are playing "My mama and hey, baby, yagga dagga dagga." Because the worse you sound now, the more successful you are. But it wasn't like that. It had to be exact and perfect. Balance, tonation, everything. You get them guys, the Skyrise or Tramps or them funny names, them guys, and the broads singing "Baby, baby, my man done me wrong," it's ridiculous. They get a $3.00 guitar, hair long, sing, "the wind is blowing, the water's wet."
